DFW6 simulation · September 14, 2026 · Completed experiments

Picking, putaway
and the traffic between them

A controlled comparison of inventory starting state, order release timing and synthetic induction policy, with physical completion counts and cell-level traffic evidence.

Generated 2026-09-14T05:19:48.578571-07:00. 12 recordings analyzed; 0 queued/running; 0 awaiting audit; 4 expected stock-preflight rejections; 0 run/analysis failures or audit discrepancies. Source dd6ef9096. Seed 0. All orders retained.

FindingsMatrixSource filesCongestionControls & limitationsRun evidence

What the evidence supports

  • Full preload, T0 orders: 1245.1 picked units/h over 16.00h; peak full hour 1,415.
  • Partial preload with putaway: 1249.6 picked units/h over 16.00h; peak full hour 1,391.
  • Empty start, order-priority induction: 228.8 picked units/h over 16.00h; peak full hour 239.
  • Partial preload sustained picking while replenishing: 20,939 units inducted (1308.7/h) and 4,087 filled totes stored (255.4/h), with pick throughput +0.36% relative to full preload. HTM busy time rose from 63.9% to 70.5%; VTM busy time from 50.2% to 55.7%. This single-seed comparison also changes stock quantity and placement, so the small pick-rate difference is not an isolated causal effect of putaway.
  • Operator headroom remains: the full and partial runs completed 1198.4 and 1210.8 transfer tasks/h, respectively—83.2% and 84.1% of the zero-loss service bound. Multi-unit transfers explain why units/hour looks closer to 1,440 than task service does.
  • Inbound sequence matters more than total inbound units in the empty-start tests: order-priority sequencing produced 3,660 picks, compared with 32 under demand-ranked SKU sequencing over the same 16h. The two runs inducted 12,499 and 19,128 units, respectively. Supplying many units does not help an assigned order whose required SKU is still absent.
  • Full preload with source timing: 25,625 units picked in 47.32h; peak full-hour throughput 1,290 at T=20–21h. The extraction journal records 22,160 completed order-container extractions and 25,625 extracted units. The overall 541.6/h average includes the sparse start and late arrivals. The run stopped before its 52h limit after finishing the workload.
  • Timed empty start exposes blocking in order assignment: 1,696 units picked in 52h, with a peak full hour of 293. At the endpoint, 169 assigned orders needed a SKU never yet inducted, while 11,079 released, unassigned orders were individually stock-ready. Median assignment wait was 22.2h. This directly supports an assignment/induction mismatch; it is not evidence that traffic congestion caused the collapse. The stock-ready candidates can compete for the same units.
  • A synthetic one-hour inbound lead did not resolve timed empty-start starvation: 1,237 units picked in the first 16h (77.3/h), versus 1,450 (90.6/h) when all order-priority lots were eligible from T0. Its peak was higher (370/h), but the sustained outcome was worse. Peak throughput alone misses the later starvation.

These are simulation experiments, not a certified warehouse capacity or congestion assessment. The physical VTM model, decant behavior and outbound simplifications still differ from the proposed installation. A valid run can measure the implemented model while leaving those site questions open.

The earlier eight-hour partial-preload experiment completed 9,651 picks (1,206.4/h), 10,719 inducted units (1,339.9/h), 2,058 filled totes and 2,052 completed rack stores. Its full-preload/no-putaway baseline completed 9,549 picks (1,193.6/h). Peak full-hour picks were 1,242 and 1,246 respectively. This is encouraging shared-fleet behavior; it is not a clean estimate of putaway’s isolated effect because preload quantity and stock placement also changed.

The earlier empty-start run completed only 28 picks in eight hours. Its synthetic induction ranked SKUs by total file demand, while orders were assigned by ID. This mismatch delayed required SKUs by thousands of induction lots. The new comparison retains that policy as a control and tests order-priority sequencing explicitly.

Cold-start supply has a separate capacity limit. With one SKU per synthetic inbound tote and at most six units per fill, the file requires at least 21,182 demand-serving fills. Six stations at 60 fills/hour need at least 58.8 hours of ideal induction to supply all requested units from empty, before transport losses. Inducting the entire on-hand snapshot needs at least 329,814 fills (916.2 hours at that ideal rate). These bounds apply to the current single-SKU-per-fill synthetic model. General inventory supports mixed-SKU totes, but synthetic decant does not yet generate mixed-SKU fills. Raising the unit cap alone barely changes the distinct-SKU requirement. These are cumulative service lower bounds, not predictions of a peak hourly pick rate. Partial preload leaves only 378 demanded units missing, so it tests a fundamentally different starting condition.

“Order-priority” orders the inbound lots by source release then order ID, or order ID alone for T0 experiments. Preloaded units and surplus from earlier lots cover demand before another priority lot is generated. All lots are available for induction at T0 unless the explicit one-hour lead sensitivity is selected. Availability does not teleport inventory: empty-tote retrieval, decant, HTM travel and VTM rack storage still take physical time.

Static induction and live order assignment are not identical policies. The order dispatcher chooses the earliest eligible assignment time and then order ID. Once several orders are already released, their IDs determine priority; the induction queue remains sorted by original release time. The source-timed empty-start case can therefore develop another supply/assignment mismatch as backlog grows. The T0 case shares ID priority. These experiments test a fixed induction sequence, not dynamic reprioritization for the currently assigned orders. Any resulting throughput loss must be distinguished from congestion.

Queue sizing and what the WIP measurements mean

The implemented pipeline ceiling is ceil(queue_factor × F_max / service_period) + 2. With queue factor 3, a roughly 133-second estimated fetch path and a 10-second operator period, the station limits are 42–43 inventory visits. The two extra credits are the existing presentation/estimation margin. This is a sizing heuristic; it does not guarantee saturation when shared robots, stock or traffic add delays.

Little’s law relates observed mean WIP, throughput and mean residence time for the same population and stage. A logical inventory credit, a loaded HTM approaching the conveyor, a tote on the conveyor, and an order HTM inside its waiting area are different populations. Each has a separate count and lifetime here. Physical order-area admission remains limited to six residents per side, regardless of how much upstream work is prepared.

For example, EasyLoop 1 in the partial/T0 run averaged 3.07 loaded inventory HTMs awaiting boarding, with 301.1 boardings/hour. Dividing that WIP by the completion rate gives about 36.7s in this stage, close to the directly observed completed-visit mean of 36.6s. The small difference includes startup and unfinished visits at the boundary. This is the stage-specific comparison relevant to robot occupancy; the roughly 42 logical credits include earlier preparation waiting.

Partial preload masks some induction-policy problems

With source order timing, order-priority, demand-ranked and one-hour-lead induction averaged 624.2, 618.9 and 616.1 picks/hour over 16h. The differences are small in this window, because preload already covers most demand.

The one-hour-lead case carries very little inbound work: it inducted only 139 units, compared with 19,546 under T0-eligible order-priority induction and 19,130 under demand-ranked induction. Only the remaining order shortages receive priority lots. The FIFO sequence leaves the bulk surplus behind later priority lots whose release time has not arrived. This case therefore cannot establish simultaneous high-rate picking and putaway capacity.

The demand-ranked case nevertheless ended with 46 assigned orders still unprepared; 43 lacked sufficient unreserved stock. Their median assignment wait was 2.73h, while 66 released, unassigned orders were individually stock-ready. Near-baseline aggregate throughput can coexist with starvation of particular orders. A longer full-file partial-preload run remains necessary after fixing this policy.

With partial preload and all orders at T0, demand-ranked induction produced 19,849 picks (1240.6/h), compared with 19,993 (1249.6/h) under order-priority induction. Inducted volumes were 19,979 and 20,939 units respectively. These measurements use the same preload and sixteen-hour horizon.

The T0 demand-ranked case ended with 12 assigned, unprepared orders, of which 9 lacked sufficient unreserved stock. Its headline rate therefore needs to be read alongside the remaining order backlog.

Extended source-timed runs

What the supplied files actually say

Stock is a starting snapshot

onhand.csv contains 174,997 SKUs and 1,397,589 units. Fields include item dimensions, velocity band and on_hand_qty. It contains no induction, receiving, ASN, truck-arrival or tote-location timestamps. The approved demo overlay adds 43 units across 40 SKUs, yielding 1,397,632 units.

The snapshot does not specify how stock is divided among physical totes. Automatic preload distributes it across eligible rack totes; mixed SKUs and multiple units are allowed. Empty start means empty source totes already exist in the racks, not an empty building with no containers.

Orders have release times

outbound.csv contains 22,160 orders, 24,789 lines and 25,625 requested units, covering 21,161 SKUs. Drops span 2026-08-13T00:11:27 through 2026-08-14T23:28:09—47.28 hours. No timezone offset is present.

Only 245 orders arrive in the first six hours. Every order’s lines agree on its drop timestamp. cutoff_time contains time-of-day values without a date; its precise operational meaning and relationship to truck release are unconfirmed. Buffer hold in these experiments is a synthetic one hour after storage.

Automatic preload uses 162,060 stocked inventory totes for the full snapshot, averaging 8.62 units each. Partial preload uses 81,030 stocked totes, averaging 9.22 units each. The map exposes 174,020 source storage positions. The configured 100 units/tote is a packing limit; it does not mean every preloaded tote contains 100 units. The loader spreads the finite stock across its selected totes.

Sending the two files together establishes neither an inbound schedule nor a cold-start commissioning sequence. We synthesize inbound work by subtracting preload from the on-hand snapshot. Full preload leaves no inbound work; partial leaves 650,389 units; empty leaves all 1,397,632 units to induct. With putaway disabled, partial stock is 378 units short across 321 required SKUs, and empty stock cannot satisfy any order.

Order mix: 20,513 single-unit orders and 1,647 multiple-unit orders; 1,334 multiline orders. Containers: {'bag': 10194, 'box': 10415, 'SIOC': 1551}. Destinations: {'SC': 3545, 'DS': 14626, '3P': 3989}. This mixture matters: early T0 tests disproportionately exercise single-unit orders because internal IDs follow source-ID string order.

Observed traffic and congestion questions

RunHoursTravel-cell waiting (HTM-h)Share of total fleet-timeMoving exposure (HTM-h)Moving mean (m/s)Moving time below 1m/s
Full preload · no putaway1673.672.00%681.52.5923.7%
Partial · order-priority putaway1674.622.03%732.52.5723.7%
Empty · order-priority putaway161.510.04%203.12.8618.9%
Partial · source-timed orders1628.580.78%416.92.5923.6%

The two saturated-order tests accumulated 73.67 and 74.62 HTM-hours of ordinary travel-cell waiting. Adding putaway increased movement exposure, while mean moving speed stayed close: 2.59 versus 2.57m/s. The fleet-wide averages therefore show no broad collapse in this comparison.

The station apron still warrants attention. In the partial-preload run, the largest waiting total was cell c874, at (47.3, 13.2)m: 6.23 HTM-hours, or 39.0% of the observation window. Adjacent apron cells recur among the largest hotspots in both high-load runs. These waits are explicit recorded waits; reasons can include station admission and reserved traffic. Their totals alone cannot separate the two causes.

The high-load speed distribution has substantial slow and fast exposure: 23.7% of moving time below 1m/s and 33.3% between 4 and 4.5m/s. This is consistent with a mixture of acceleration, crossing/turning approaches and straight travel; it does not establish that slow waves interrupt fast waves. The next traffic diagnosis should inspect direction and time around the apron hotspots.

A high-volume map can have a local choke point while much of the fleet is idle. Conversely, low throughput can come from missing stock or unreleased orders while travel cells are clear. We therefore examine local waiting exposure, moving-speed distributions, inventory residence before conveyor boarding, order residence and final-pick-to-exit delay together.

  • Stationary waiting: measured in HTM-seconds per cell. Queue, presentation/access, exchange and charging cells are excluded from the travel-cell color scale. Eligible waiting still includes waiting for work or resources; causal labels are incomplete.
  • Moving speed: distance divided by moving time, with duration-weighted 0.5m/s bins. Stops and turns in place are excluded and measured separately. The median is reported as a containing bin, not an exact value.
  • Spatial attribution: each link contributes half its distance to each endpoint cell. Canonical kinematics, including curves, determine the time split. This avoids treating rendering samples as measurements.
  • Window and exposure: hotspot comparisons use the common first-16h window. The report shows time exposure beside speed; a cell observed for two seconds cannot carry the same confidence as an aisle observed for hours.
  • What a cumulative map cannot prove: two speed populations do not establish interference. Distinct fast and slow waves can be healthy. Directional, time-resolved crossing analysis and reliable wait-cause attribution remain necessary to diagnose that mechanism.

Each completed run below contains its own waiting map and hotspot table. Exact raw cell IDs, entity identities, coordinates, moving-time histograms and implicit idle holds are retained in its traffic JSON. Canonical movement is checked against playback duration. Low observed waiting in this model cannot clear the proposed layout of floor-driving-VTM or real robot-clearance risks. The report is rendered and checked in a headless browser. Production metric, serialization, tooltip-unit and shader checks have passed; a final visual acceptance of the desvis GPU heatmap itself remains outstanding.

The audit found that some declared waiting berths have an ordinary Open traversal type. The UI source and report exporter now exclude them by equipment membership. The frozen simulation executable predates that UI fix; its simulation physics and recorded movements were preserved for comparison. Rebuild the headed application before the remaining visual heatmap check.

Fixed controls, capacity bounds and open questions

ControlValue and interpretation
Robots230 HTMs; 40 inventory VTMs plus 8 buffer VTMs. The extra buffer fleet remains a site clarification. The DoO lists a different total VTM count; do not silently reconcile incompatible document revisions.
PickingFour EasyLoops, one exclusive operator each, two presentation sides, six waiting positions per side. Ten seconds per implemented item-transfer task; 1,440 transfers/hour is the zero-loss four-operator bound. Multiple units can move in one task, so 1,440 is not a universal units/hour ceiling. Unit-dependent handling time remains to be calibrated.
Inbound / decantSix stations; provisional 60 tote fills/hour/station; at most six units in a same-SKU inbound lot. Ideal bound: 360 filled totes/hour and at most 2,160 units/hour before transport losses or partial lots. A different DoO figure is 250 units/hour/station. Multiple active decant positions, top-off workflow and inbound-case delivery are not fully represented.
InventoryFinite on-hand snapshot, no fabricated replacement supply. Initial plus future stock passes the order sufficiency check. A 1.4-million-unit empty start is a very large replenishment problem; eight or sixteen hours cannot recreate the original stock snapshot at these rates.
Queueing / admissionQueue factor 3. Logical assignments can exceed the 12 physical order residents per EasyLoop. Physical admission is time-reserved. Inventory release has its own CONWIP bound and consumer timing. WIP must be measured in consistent units before applying a rate × residence-time relationship.
Order containers / outbound128 reusable SIOC trays for diagnostic continuity (not a validated site count); ordinary order totes form a separate seeded pool. This does not cap all reusable containers at 128. Ordinary box induction and extraction enabled. Boxes disappear at sealer handoff; sealed-box reinduction is deferred. DS uses the buffer with a one-hour hold; SC direct extraction remains temporary. Tote/tray contents leave at extraction and the container returns to storage.
Motion and trafficKinematic HTM motion and collision avoidance always enabled. Relay entry/back-out and rotation restrictions are modeled. Walmart floor-driving VTMs are not implemented; charging and battery constraints are not modeled. Reservation-based navigation does not establish real-world safety or physical throughput.
ReproducibilityOne frozen release binary and copied inputs, seed 0, no order cap. Its hash and simulation source commit are frozen in the manifest; profile Git metadata is collected at runtime and may reflect later report-only commits. At most four headless runs, RAM-gated. No headed windows launched. One seed is a controlled comparison, not a confidence interval.

Questions that materially change the result

  1. What is the actual inbound receiving/decant schedule, and is the on-hand snapshot already present at the first order drop?
  2. Should orders lacking allocatable stock remain unassigned, or should decant prioritize inventory for already-assigned orders? Should released orders retain earliest-release priority instead of switching to ID priority when a backlog exists?
  3. What are the validated decant presentation count, units per tote, active positions, top-off policy and service-time distribution?
  4. What is the operator time for multiple units versus one unit, including confirmation and switching sides?
  5. What event releases buffered orders, and what do cutoff_time, destination_type and truck timing mean operationally?
  6. What are the floor-driving VTM fleet, aisle rules and shared-traffic footprint? What order-tray count and charging workload should be modeled?

Recommended next experiments

  1. Remove inventory starvation from order assignment. Compare stock-ready admission or induction that prioritizes assigned shortages against the frozen baseline. Preserve physical order-area admission limits and use simulator timestamps for availability. Measure waiting assigned orders and stock-ready unassigned orders alongside picks.
  2. Calibrate inbound workload. Obtain actual receiving times and tote contents, then compare the site decant workflow with the current single-SKU synthetic fills. Keep empty-start commissioning separate from steady operation with working inventory.
  3. Explain operator idle time and apron waiting together. Attribute each idle interval to order-container readiness, inventory readiness, conveyor/side availability or outbound clearance. Inspect traffic directions and time windows at the identified apron cells before increasing release rates or fleet size.
  4. Repeat the selected correction. Use the same stock placement and workload for an isolated comparison, then additional seeds and a longer horizon to check that gains persist. Reintroduce the floor-driving VTM footprint and validated charging/inbound/outbound details before drawing site-capacity conclusions.

Earlier isolation experiments

Before the present outbound layout and buffer corrections, an eight-hour inventory-release run averaged 891.5 picks/h; a one-hour run with extraction bypassed achieved 1,264; an eight-hour run bypassing both extraction and box induction averaged 1,339.25. An earlier VTM-isolation run achieved 635.4/h. These are historical diagnostic results with different code/layout controls, not rows in this matched experiment or evidence that bypasses solve the physical design.

Run evidence and configurations

All rates count physical completions through the relevant observation boundary. Inducted units, filled totes and filled-tote rack stores are separate events. Error and preflight cases are retained. Evidence links point to local artifacts; the embedded tables and charts remain readable when this HTML is shared alone.

Iteration 47: partial-on-source-sku_demand

Partial preload · putaway on · original order drop times · requested 16h.

Execution: 83.2 wall-clock minutes; peak sampled resident memory 12.29 GiB. Samples can miss shorter memory peaks.

9,902 units picked in 16.00h (618.9/h overall). Peak full hour: 1,272 at T=14–15h. Best rolling 60-minute count: 1,292. 192 transfer events moved more than one unit.

Reported fleet idle: HTM 34.0%, VTM 68.0%. First-16h idle from integrated duty intervals: HTM 34.0%, VTM 68.0%. Idle is time outside tracked busy states, not all stationary time or proof that an HTM is unladen and immediately reusable. Instantaneous state-count snapshots are not used to estimate fleet-time shares.

9,672 completed transfer tasks (604.5/h), or 42.0% of the four-operator, ten-second service bound. This measures completed service against the bound; it excludes any partially completed service at the endpoint. Picked units can exceed the transfer count when one task moves several units.
